claims.text: A conventional tempered martensitic steel will display a ductile–brittle–ductile transition when thermally cycled through a narrow temperature window.
The transition occurs because embrittling impurities segregate to grain boundaries only over a limited temperature range.
The initial tempered martensitic steel has a homogeneous distribution of alloying and minor impurity elements.
The initial tempered martensitic steel is ductile at room temperature.
Phosphorus, antimony, or tin can segregate to grain boundaries in the proposed steel.
Grain-boundary segregation of embrittling species compromises intergranular cohesion.
At intermediate temperatures, the mobility of embrittling elements increases.
Increased mobility at intermediate temperatures causes preferential segregation of embrittling elements at grain boundaries.
Preferential grain-boundary segregation induces a brittle state.
At high temperatures, segregation is insufficient to sustain embrittlement.
At low temperatures, the activity of embrittling species is frozen.
The steel regains ductility at temperatures outside the intermediate embrittlement window.
The steel will have high ductility at both high and low temperatures.
The steel will exhibit a marked reduction in ductility within a narrow intermediate-temperature range.
The steel will exhibit a marked reduction in fracture toughness within the same narrow intermediate-temperature range.
The proposed behavior is specific to conventional low- or intermediate-complexity alloys that permit impurity segregation.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys lack pronounced temper embrittlement.
Compositionally complex or high-entropy alloys will not exhibit the proposed ductile–brittle–ductile transition.
Transition temperatures and the magnitude of ductility loss depend on impurity content and alloy composition.
Processing variability can affect grain-boundary segregation behavior.

contradictions.description: The intervention is described as thermal cycling through the embrittlement window, but the proposed low-temperature recovery is attributed to impurity activity being frozen. If impurities segregate during the intermediate-temperature portion of a cycle, freezing at low temperature would not by itself remove that segregation or explain recovery of ductility.
